text: Everything so far has been about getting the past right — matching what already happened against the bank's record of it. Cash Positioning looks at today and the very near future: how much cash does the company actually have, account by account, right now?

A cash position is a bank account by account view of beginning balance, inflows, outflows, and a projected balance, typically for today or the next several days. Unlike a forecast, which can run months out, a position is deliberately short horizon and built from real, mostly already known activity rather than long range projection.

It's built from three things: the bank's own reported balance from the most recent statement, reconciled transactions already confirmed against the bank, and transactions still open but expected imminently, like a payment run scheduled for today. Because it leans on real statement balances, a position is only as reliable as the reconciliation work behind it.

Treasury uses this to make same-day or same-week decisions: does an account have surplus worth sweeping into an investment? Does another account need a transfer in before a payroll run clears? Positioning is short horizon and transaction grounded — what do I actually have. Forecasting, next lesson, looks further out and leans more on projection — what should I expect.

A fictional example: Harborview Metals Inc's Treasury team reviews Monday's position, projects to $150,000 by Friday, comfortably above their $100,000 minimum balance — so no transfer needed this week. Up next, lesson eighteen: Cash Forecasting, which takes a longer view.
